doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

title: Thinking while playing: presence, meditation and humility
summary: The best nights are when she is not thinking; she values collective improvisation and humility.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: What do you think about when you play?

Well the best night is where I’m not thinking. And that goes back to that idea of Satori, the concept of presence. And that’s I think where I find the most freedom and the most – oh yeah that sense of just being right here right now. It sort of transcends all of the other © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

stuff that one has to think about. And I’m a very undisciplined and not very good meditator. I don’t like sitting still and I get very impatient and I know many people probably are going yes, that is what meditation is. But to me I think that that sense of being in a meditative state comes when I’m really in the music either listening or performing. And it’s so satisfying. However, it’s not always that kind of slow state, as I think some people call it. Sometimes I am thinking and that can be quite distracting. For example, “Ooh I want this to be good.” And that’s a terrible thing to think because there’s so much pressure on you, and then you’re not responding. You’re thinking what can I do here that would sound good, rather than what can I do here that would sound like the right thing to do here. And maybe it’s nothing. Maybe it’s silence or maybe it’s one note or maybe it’s just the root of whatever else is happening. You’re not just adding to the whole soundscape rather than going ooh, what impressive things do I know on the saxophone. That’s the worst possible thing that I could be thinking. But it’s hard to just let that go. That’s part of the spiritual and musical development isn’t it? Letting go of the need to do anything except see what the right thing is to do in the moment.

Yeah, or to be the director of what’s going on here. I had this impression as you were talking like if you’re thinking too hard it’s actually like you’re trying to shape this music by yourself and maybe you’re not paying close attention to your bandmates.

Yeah. Exactly. Yeah. And especially with this kind of music. There is more open and free and more about the sort of collective improvisation. I think there’s a real sense of the more humble you can be and the less egotistic, the better the overall experience will be for the listener. And it’s remembering that sense of why we’re doing what we’re doing and what we might give rather than what can I show off about. I’m being facetious but I think having that sense of humility can be a really great starting point.
